# Google Meet's AI Notetaker Now Works for In-Person Meetings — Here's What Changes

> **In short:** Google Meet's "Take Notes for me" feature, which used to work only inside video calls, now also runs for in-person meetings. You start a session from your phone or laptop, the AI listens to the room through your microphone, and you get a written summary afterward.

You've just walked out of a 45-minute meeting. Your head is full of decisions, action items, and one name you can't quite remember. By the time you sit down to write notes, half of it has already faded.

Google Meet's new "Take Notes for me" feature is built for exactly this moment. After months of working only inside video calls, it's now expanding to the kind of meetings most of us actually have — the ones in conference rooms, kitchens, and coffee shops, where everyone is sitting around the same table.

## What's actually new

Until recently, "Take Notes for me" lived inside a Google Meet video call. You'd click a button in the meeting window, the AI would join as a silent participant, and at the end you'd get a summary, key points, and suggested action items.

Now Google is rolling out the same idea for in-person meetings. Instead of needing a video call, you start a "Take Notes" session directly from the Google Meet home screen on web or mobile. The session runs locally — no video, no remote participants required — and the AI listens through your device's microphone.

When the session ends, you get the same kind of structured notes the video version produces: a summary, decisions, and any to-dos the AI can spot from what was said.

## How it works in practice

You open the Google Meet app or visit meet.google.com on the web. On the home screen, alongside the usual "Start a meeting" or "Join with a code" options, you'll see a "Take Notes" button.

Tap it, name the session, and start. Place your phone on the table or keep your laptop open. The AI listens in real time and turns spoken conversation into notes. When the meeting wraps up, you stop the session and the notes appear, ready to share, edit, or save.

A small heads-up: features like this usually roll out gradually. If you don't see the "Take Notes" button on your home screen yet, check back in a week or two — and if you're using Google Workspace for work, your admin may need to enable it for your account first.

## What this means for you

- **If you run or attend lots of work meetings**: this is one of the most useful AI tools to land in the productivity space in a while. You stay focused on the conversation instead of juggling a laptop and a notebook. The notes land shortly after, with action items already pulled out.
- **If you take minutes for a club, team, or volunteer group**: this saves real time. The AI does the first draft of the minutes; you just edit and send.
- **If you're worried about privacy**: the feature is off by default — you choose when to start it. The notes are saved to your own Google account, not shared automatically, and anyone in the room can see that a session is running, so a quick heads-up to the group is the polite move.
- **If you're just curious about AI assistants**: this is a good example of how AI is moving beyond chatbots into the background of everyday tasks. You don't type a prompt. You don't even look at it. It just works while you talk.

## Wrap-up

The idea behind "Take Notes for me" isn't really about taking notes. It's about being fully present in the room while still having a clean record of what happened. For anyone who has ever left a meeting with a half-empty notebook and a fuzzy memory, that's a meaningful change.

A simple step to try today: open Google Meet on your phone or laptop and look for the "Take Notes" button on the home screen. If it's there, run a short test session during your next meeting — even a quick 15-minute one — and see how the summary comes out.
